title: Energy policy still serves corporate interests, CAB dialogue hears
excerpt: Speakers at a Consumers Association of Bangladesh dialogue said import dependence and private interests still outweigh public interest in energy policy.
content:
Successive governments have failed to change an energy model built on costly projects, imports and corporate interests, speakers said at a dialogue organised by the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB) in Dhaka on Thursday (26 November), The Daily Star reported.

The dialogue, "Public Interest in Energy Transition: Justice, Accountability and Legal Struggle", was held at Bishwo Shahitto Kendro. Economist Anu Muhammad said energy policy had shifted towards import dependence and profit-driven investment. "When we talk about developing local experts and enhancing the capacity of the national exploration company, lack of funds is shown as the main issue. But when it comes to imports, we don't have a shortage of funds," he said.

He said poor planning and weak infrastructure had also put lives at risk, citing gas explosions, adulterated fuel and accidents on electricity distribution lines. CAB energy adviser Prof M Shamsul Alam called for a new citizens' platform led by young people and students to challenge decisions against the public interest.

Prof Mohammad Tanjimuddin Khan of Dhaka University's Department of International Relations said energy transition should go beyond replacing fossil fuels with renewables and should change who owns, invests, profits and bears risk. He criticised capacity payments and the agreement with India's Adani Power, saying changes of government had not changed how the state makes energy decisions.

Why it matters

Energy costs reach every household and programme, through electricity tariffs, fuel prices and subsidies that compete with health and education in the budget. The World Bank's Bangladesh Public Finance Review 2026, published on 19 November, says power and gas subsidies are adding to the strain on public money available for development. A recent study found 92% of energy climate finance comes as loans, which matters for how a renewable transition will be paid for.

What to watch

  • Electricity and gas tariff decisions by the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission.
  • Any review of capacity payments or the Adani Power contract.
